title: National Labor Relations Board v. Wyman-Gordon Co.
lead: A labor board announces a future voter-list requirement, then orders Wyman-Gordon to comply in its own election. Seven Justices enforce the particular order, while dividing over whether the earlier policy was validly adopted.

actors.name: National Labor Relations Board
actors.role: Federal agency supervising representation elections and seeking disclosure enforcement.

actors.name: Wyman-Gordon Company
actors.role: Employer that twice refused employee voter lists.

actors.name: Boilermakers and the other election union
actors.role: Unions seeking representation and access to eligible voters.

actors.name: Excelsior employers and unions
actors.role: Parties to the earlier two-company election controversy that produced the prospective disclosure requirement.

proceedings: After both unions lost an election without the list, the Board ordered a new election and again required disclosure.
The District of Massachusetts enforced the Board’s subpoena or mandatory demand, 270 F. Supp. 280 (1967).
The Supreme Court reversed on April 23, 1969, directing reinstatement of the district-court enforcement judgment.
limits: This historical source-brief transformation makes no new audit or later-law claim. Seven Justices agreed on enforcement, disclosure’s substance and subpoena authority, not Fortas’s entire rationale. Four plurality Justices and two dissenters criticized Excelsior’s adoption but disagreed on the remedy. The prior Excelsior adjudication involved two companies.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Excelsior announces a disclosure policy but protects its original parties from it
sections.cue: What future obligation emerged from the earlier election disputes?
paragraphs: In Excelsior Underwear, the National Labor Relations Board considered unions’ objections after losing representation elections at two companies that refused to provide employee names and addresses. The Board invited selected employer organizations and unions to brief and argue the broader disclosure question.

In 1966 it announced that employers must file eligible voters’ names and addresses with the regional director within seven days after approval of an election agreement or direction of an election. The director would make the information available to election parties, and noncompliance could support setting aside an election upon proper objections.

The Board did not apply the new requirement to the two original employers. It covered only elections directed or agreed to more than thirty days after the decision. That prospective limitation, later understood by Justice Black as protecting reliance on previous decisions against compelled disclosure, created the rulemaking-versus-adjudication dispute in Wyman-Gordon.

sources.pinpoint: Elections and earlier Excelsior; Black concurrence; 394 U.S. 762–763, 773–774

sections.title: Wyman-Gordon refuses the list in two successive election orders
sections.cue: How did the dispute reach a court before the second election?
paragraphs: On the Boilermakers’ petition, the Board directed an election among Wyman-Gordon production and maintenance employees, who could select either of two unions or neither. The order required a list of eligible voters’ names and addresses so the unions could contact them. Wyman-Gordon refused, and both unions lost.

The Board sustained union objections based on the missing list and ordered another election, again specifically requiring disclosure within seven days for all election parties. Wyman-Gordon again refused. The Board subpoenaed the list or the underlying personnel and payroll records containing the information.

The Board sought subpoena enforcement or a mandatory injunction in the District of Massachusetts, which ordered compliance in 1967. The First Circuit reversed in 1968 because the direction rested on an improperly adopted general rule. The Supreme Court granted review amid disagreement among circuits. The employer separately disputed both disclosure’s substantive validity and whether a voter list qualified as subpoenaable evidence.

sources.pinpoint: Elections and litigation; Disclosure and subpoena; 394 U.S. 761–762, 766, 768–769

sections.title: Fortas rejects Excelsior’s rulemaking method but upholds the specific direction
sections.cue: Why did the plurality distinguish a precedent from an independently binding future rule?
paragraphs: Justice Fortas, joined by Chief Justice Warren and Justices Stewart and White, reasoned that § 6 of the National Labor Relations Act required rules to be made through the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The APA’s definition covered agency statements of general or particular applicability and future effect; § 553 imposed publication, participation, explanation and adoption-publication requirements. Selected amici did not replace Federal Register notice to all interested people, and the adopted command had not been published there. The plurality treated disclosure as substantive, outside interpretive-rule, policy-statement and procedural exceptions.

The government acknowledged omission of rulemaking but relied on compliance with adjudicatory procedures. Fortas distinguished deciding whether a particular employer must disclose from Excelsior’s prospective command not imposed on its own parties. Adjudication could create policy and precedent for later action; that did not automatically create a legislative rule binding the public without further agency action.

Wyman-Gordon nevertheless received its own express disclosure direction in the election order. Fortas regarded that direction as a valid adjudicatory order despite its reliance on Excelsior. Without the particular direction, neither statute nor a valid rule independently compelled this employer. The plurality thus enforced the specific obligation while denying independent legislative force to the earlier command.

sections.title: The plurality rejects remand and seven Justices approve disclosure and subpoena power
sections.cue: Why was the result not merely an invitation for the Board to decide again?
paragraphs: Justice Harlan argued that Chenery I’s requirement to review an agency on its own grounds required remand after rejection of its stated premise. In footnote 6, Fortas called that step futile here. Chenery concerned incorrect standards in complex facts with unresolved alternatives; Fortas considered this disclosure order’s substance incontestable and the same result certain whether the Board used rule or order. That disputed, case-specific futility rationale did not permit courts universally to invent replacement agency reasons.

The Board had broad authority to protect fair, free choice of bargaining representatives. Lists informed voters and gave unions access comparable to management’s existing access. The Board could balance solicitation burdens against those interests. Justice Black expressly agreed with this substantive conclusion.

The employer also argued that voter lists were not evidence within the National Labor Relations Act’s § 11 subpoena authority. The Court read evidence to include books, records and papers assisting an investigation, beyond proof formally introduced at a hearing. Names and addresses were within that scope. The First Circuit had not reached this separate objection; the Supreme Court decided it. Black, Brennan and Marshall joined Fortas’s Parts II and III, supplying seven votes for substantive disclosure and subpoena authority.

sources.pinpoint: Fortas remand discussion; Disclosure’s merits and subpoena; Judgment and rationales; 394 U.S. 766–770 & nn.6–8

sections.title: Black views the prospective Excelsior disposition as valid adjudication
sections.cue: Why did he reject both the plurality’s criticism and its cure?
paragraphs: Justice Black, joined by Justices Brennan and Marshall, concurred in the result because he found no adoption defect. He objected to condemning a rule as illegally adopted and then enforcing it, which he thought weakened judicial enforcement of procedural statutes.

Under Chenery II, agencies ordinarily choose whether to develop policy through adjudication or rulemaking where both fit. A decision can derive new doctrine from a statute and guide future behavior through precedent. Representation certifications were exempt from the APA’s formal adjudication requirements; the pertinent labor-statute procedures governed, so Black was not demanding every APA trial formality for elections.

Excelsior had resolved actual union objections to specific elections, rejecting the requested new elections because retroactive disclosure would upset justified reliance. Explaining a prospective requirement while denying present relief remained adjudication. Otherwise an agency would have to impose unfair retroactivity or duplicate a completed inquiry through rulemaking. Whether retroactivity was unfair might emerge only after considering the case, so Black opposed requiring an advance commitment to apply any new doctrine retroactively.

sections.title: Douglas and Harlan would require the Board to honor rulemaking limits
sections.cue: What did the final vote restore, and what remained divided?
paragraphs: Justice Douglas would affirm the First Circuit. The Board had chosen a general policy for future elections and owed public notice and participation; a thirty-day effective-date delay was no substitute. Wider participation could correct agency assumptions and give less represented groups a voice, as public comments on highway regulations illustrated. Announcing a broad rule and then using individual enforcement orders would evade Congress’s procedure. His notes criticized the Board’s historical avoidance of rulemaking and addressed exceptions.

Justice Harlan also distinguished a particular order from a future rule not applied to the originating parties. A change significant enough to make retroactivity unfair was especially suited to broad participation. He treated disclosure as substantive, not an exempt procedural rule. Under Chenery I, the regional official’s refusal to reconsider because Excelsior bound him, followed by the Board’s refusal of review, could not be replaced by a court’s confidence about a hypothetical new decision.

At minimum Harlan wanted actual reconsideration of competing interests; he would go further and require rulemaking because the Board itself rejected retroactive operation. A court could not know what renewed deliberation would produce. He therefore would affirm rather than restore enforcement on a judicial substitute rationale.

On April 23, 1969, the Court reversed and remanded to the district court with directions to reinstate the district court’s enforcement judgment. Seven Justices supported that outcome, but only four used Fortas’s invalid-rule/valid-order route; three sustained Excelsior as adjudication. Agreement between the plurality and dissenters on criticism of adoption did not yield agreement about the consequence. The source’s separate assigned discussions following Chenery I and Chenery II concern this same fractured historical decision, not additional holdings or later-case certification.
